summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would give the Secretary of the Department of Veterans' Affairs express legal authority to act, on behalf of the Commonwealth, as an agent for an insurer.

It would insert a new Part VIA into the Defence Service Homes Act 1918 allowing the Commonwealth to enter arrangements with an insurer, sell its policies, handle claims and renew or terminate policies.
It would also validate everything the Commonwealth has done as an insurer's agent under the Defence Service Home Insurance brand since 1 January 1990, commencing the day after Royal Assent.
changes: A new section 39 would let the Secretary do anything necessary or convenient to carry out insurance activities for the Commonwealth, including collecting, using and disclosing personal information.
Section 6A would be amended so the Secretary's powers under the new Part could be delegated.
The Commonwealth and the Secretary would be deemed to have held the new powers since 1 January 1990, and past arrangements with insurers would be treated as valid and effective for all purposes.
The validation would not disturb rights or liabilities that a court has already decided in concluded proceedings.
Where the validation amounts to an acquisition of property, the Commonwealth would pay reasonable compensation, with the Federal Court able to set the amount if the parties cannot agree.
summary.affected: The Department of Veterans' Affairs, its insurance partner and current and past Defence Service Home Insurance policyholders, mostly serving and former Australian Defence Force members, reservists, peacekeepers and their families, are affected.

divisions.question: The majority voted against a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2025-02-10.8.2) introduced by Tasmanian Senator [Jonathon Duniam](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/tasmania/jonathon_duniam) (Liberal), which means it failed. ### Motion text > *That so much of standing orders be suspended as would prevent me from moving a motion to provide for the consideration of a matter, namely a motion to give precedence to a motion relating to the consideration of the [Defence Service Homes Amendment (Insurance) Bill 2025](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r7304).*

speeches.speaker: Jonathon Duniam
speeches.brief: Moved to suspend standing orders and prioritise the Defence Service Homes Amendment (Insurance) Bill 2025, arguing it was urgent for affected veterans, including people impacted by flooding around Townsville; the government opposed rearranging the program, saying the bill could pass after Future Made in Australia legislation.

speeches.speaker: Penny Wong
speeches.brief: Invited the opposition to support changing the Senate program so the Defence Service Homes Amendment (Insurance) Bill 2025 and the FMIAbill could be considered and passed today, with the Senate sitting later if necessary.

speeches.speaker: Penny Wong
speeches.brief: Moved procedural motions to vary the Senate's hours and limit debate, including votes on the Future Made in Australia (Production Tax Credits and Other Measures) Bill 2024 at 8 pm and the Defence Service Homes Amendment (Insurance) Bill 2025 at 9 pm; debate criticised the government's handling of scrutiny and supported proceeding with both bills.

speeches.speaker: Perin Davey
speeches.brief: Supported the Defence Service Homes Amendment (Insurance) Bill 2025, describing it as non-controversial and necessary to resolve insurance authority issues affecting defence personnel, veterans and families. The debate also sought transparency about retrospectively validating Commonwealth activities since 1990, while the minister said the bill would formalise authority, validate past activities and support more than 32,000 current policyholders. The bill passed its second reading.
